core: What sorting is: arranging items into a predetermined order by a key
The three simple comparison sorts - bubble, insertion, selection - all O(n^2) worst and average case
That insertion sort is O(n) in the best case on nearly-sorted data
Naming the efficient sorts: merge sort O(n log n); quicksort average O(n log n), worst O(n^2)
Comparison-based sorting and the meaning of a stable sort
One traced worked example: bubble sort on [5, 2, 4, 1], pass by pass, verified in Bash
supporting: That the choice of sort depends on data size, orderliness, and the cost of comparing vs. moving items
That sorting enables efficient techniques such as binary search (one-sentence handoff)
That merge sort and quicksort are recursive (named only, recursion is its own topic)

claims.claim: To sort is to arrange items in a predetermined order; the choice of algorithm depends on factors such as the number of items relative to working memory, prior knowledge of the data's orderliness or key range, and the cost of comparing keys versus moving items.

Bubble sort compares each adjacent pair in turn, swapping when out of order, and repeats passes until a pass makes no swaps; it is O(n^2) for arbitrary data but approaches Theta(n) when the list is already nearly in order.

Insertion sort repeatedly takes the next item and inserts it into its proper place among the already-sorted items; its run time is O(n^2) because of the moves required, and it is O(n) in the best case when the input is already nearly sorted.
Selection sort repeatedly searches the remaining items for the least one and moves it to its final position; its run time is Theta(n^2), though it performs only O(n) swaps.
Merge sort splits the items into two groups, recursively sorts each group, and merges them into one sorted sequence; its run time is Theta(n log n).

Quicksort picks a pivot, partitions the remaining elements into those less than and greater than the pivot, and recursively sorts the partitions; it typically runs in O(n log n) but has Theta(n^2) worst-case running time.
A sort is stable when the relative order of items with equal keys in the input is always preserved in the output.
No comparison-based sorting algorithm can do better than O(n log n) comparisons in the worst case, and a sorted list is what makes index-based techniques like binary search possible.
Running bubble sort on [5, 2, 4, 1] yields the pass sequence [2, 4, 1, 5] then [2, 1, 4, 5] then [1, 2, 4, 5], ending in the sorted list [1, 2, 4, 5].
claims.verification: Executed and traced in Python 3 via Bash on 2026-08-19; each pass and the final result [1, 2, 4, 5] match sorted([5,2,4,1]).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether bubble sort's complexity is best written O(n^2) or Theta(n^2).
positions: NIST DADS gives bubble sort as O(n^2) for arbitrary data, approaching Theta(n) when nearly ordered.
Many texts state a tight Theta(n^2) average/worst bound for the naive version.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows NIST: worst and average case O(n^2), with a best case near Theta(n)/O(n) on nearly-sorted input for bubble and insertion sort. Selection sort is stated as Theta(n^2) in all cases, matching NIST.
